Custom Blueprint

blueprint.Rmd
library(glysmith)

A blueprint is simply an analytical plan that tells forge_analysis() what to do. By default, forge_analysis() runs a default blueprint:

blueprint_default()
#> Blueprint (root accepts exp)
#> ├─ node_1  step_ident_overview() [overview] (terminal)
#> └─ node_2  step_preprocess() (exp)
#>   ├─ node_3  step_plot_qc(when = "post") [qc] (terminal)
#>   ├─ node_4  step_pca() [scores] (terminal)
#>   ├─ node_5  step_dea_limma() [abundances] (contrast)
#>   │ ├─ node_6  step_volcano() [abundances] (terminal)
#>   │ ├─ node_7  step_filter_sig_vars() [abundances] (filtered_exp)
#>   │ │ └─ node_8  step_heatmap() [abundances] (terminal)
#>   │ ├─ node_9  step_sig_enrich_go() [abundances] (terminal)
#>   │ ├─ node_10  step_sig_enrich_kegg() [abundances] (terminal)
#>   │ └─ node_11  step_sig_enrich_reactome() [abundances] (terminal)
#>   └─ node_12  step_derive_traits() [traits] (exp)
#>     └─ node_13  step_dea_limma() [traits] (contrast)
#>       └─ node_14  step_filter_sig_vars() [traits] (filtered_exp)
#>         └─ node_15  step_heatmap() [traits] (terminal)

This vignette shows you how to build your own blueprint for custom analyses.

Heads up: Before diving into the details of manual blueprint creation, you might want to try having an LLM generate one for you with inquire_blueprint(). Check out this vignette for the details.

Connect steps by their outputs

Use %=>% to pass the output of one step to the next. Each comma-separated argument to blueprint() starts a route on the original experiment. Glysmith reserves %=>% for blueprint composition. Ordinary R and magrittr data pipelines keep their own operators. The following routes each fit one model and give its result to two consumers. Use a two-group experiment for the t-test.

dea_bp1 <- blueprint(
  step_dea_limma() %=>% fork(
    step_volcano(),
    step_filter_sig_vars() %=>% step_heatmap()
  )
)
dea_bp2 <- blueprint(
  step_dea_ttest() %=>% fork(
    step_volcano(),
    step_filter_sig_vars() %=>% step_heatmap()
  )
)

# Two independent entry routes run preprocessing twice.
independent <- blueprint(
  limma = step_preprocess() %=>% dea_bp1,
  ttest = step_preprocess() %=>% dea_bp2,
)

# One preprocessing step supplies both saved analysis routes.
shared <- blueprint(step_preprocess() %=>% fork(limma = dea_bp1, ttest = dea_bp2))
print(shared)
#> Blueprint (root accepts exp)
#> └─ node_1  step_preprocess() (exp)
#>   ├─ node_2  step_dea_limma() [limma] (contrast)
#>   │ ├─ node_3  step_volcano() [limma] (terminal)
#>   │ └─ node_4  step_filter_sig_vars() [limma] (filtered_exp)
#>   │   └─ node_5  step_heatmap() [limma] (terminal)
#>   └─ node_6  step_dea_ttest() [ttest] (contrast)
#>     ├─ node_7  step_volcano() [ttest] (terminal)
#>     └─ node_8  step_filter_sig_vars() [ttest] (filtered_exp)
#>       └─ node_9  step_heatmap() [ttest] (terminal)

Each argument of fork() receives the current output. A fork can be nested or start at the inlet, and ends its route. A side route preserves that output for the next step. For example, br("scores", step_pca()) %=>% step_dea_limma() supplies the same experiment to PCA and limma.

This blueprint derives traits once and fits ANOVA to both the abundance and trait experiments. PCA receives the same traits as the second ANOVA.

inspect_fit <- blueprint(
  step_dea_anova() %=>% fork(
    strict = step_filter_sig_vars(0.01),
    selected = step_filter_sig_vars() %=>% step_heatmap()
  )
)
traits <- step_derive_traits() %=>% fork(step_pca(), inspect_fit)
bp <- blueprint(step_preprocess() %=>% fork(abundances = inspect_fit, traits = traits))
print(bp)
#> Blueprint (root accepts exp)
#> └─ node_1  step_preprocess() (exp)
#>   ├─ node_2  step_dea_anova() [abundances] (omnibus)
#>   │ ├─ node_3  step_filter_sig_vars(p_adj_cutoff = 0.01) [abundances/strict] (filtered_exp)
#>   │ └─ node_4  step_filter_sig_vars() [abundances/selected] (filtered_exp)
#>   │   └─ node_5  step_heatmap() [abundances/selected] (terminal)
#>   └─ node_6  step_derive_traits() [traits] (exp)
#>     ├─ node_7  step_pca() [traits] (terminal)
#>     └─ node_8  step_dea_anova() [traits] (omnibus)
#>       ├─ node_9  step_filter_sig_vars(p_adj_cutoff = 0.01) [traits/strict] (filtered_exp)
#>       └─ node_10  step_filter_sig_vars() [traits/selected] (filtered_exp)
#>         └─ node_11  step_heatmap() [traits/selected] (terminal)
Step Input Main output
Preprocessing, group subsetting, structure inference, traits, motifs Experiment Transformed experiment
Limma, t-test, Wilcoxon Experiment Contrast fit
ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis Experiment Omnibus fit
step_filter_sig_vars() Either fit Filtered experiment
step_volcano() Contrast fit with abundance fold changes Terminal plot
Enrichment Fit and its bound experiment Terminal analysis
step_sig_boxplot() Filtered experiment from step_filter_sig_vars() Terminal plot
QC, PCA and other dimension reduction, heatmap, ROC, correlation, Cox and other summaries Experiment (including filtered) Terminal analysis

DEA steps fit the experiment on their incoming wire. Set cutoffs on step_filter_sig_vars(). A fit’s filter_* arguments supply defaults that each filter can override. To compare thresholds, use blueprint(step_dea_anova() %=>% fork(step_filter_sig_vars(0.01), step_filter_sig_vars(0.05))). Each filter uses the exact experiment that produced the fit. A filter that selects zero variables succeeds and returns a zero-row experiment. Downstream analyses skip an empty input. A skipped or failed step blocks its descendants, and independent branches continue.

result <- forge_analysis(glyexp::real_experiment2, bp)
result$meta$nodes        # step, producer, route, status and reason
cast_data(result)        # node outputs and auxiliary objects
cast_plot(result)        # e.g. node_5__heatmap
cast_table(result)
glyvis::autoplot(cast_data(result, "node_2"))  # abundance ANOVA main test
quench_result(result, "connected-results")
polish_report(result, "connected-report.html", open = FALSE)

Use the printed node ID to retrieve its main output, e.g. cast_data(result, "node_2"). Plot, table and auxiliary object names start with the producing node ID and two underscores. The prepared input is available as cast_data(result, "root"). For each fit, its parent ID retrieves the experiment used to fit the model. cast_exp() returns the last experiment on the main route, or the input if that route only fits or plots. With multiple top-level routes, cast_exp() returns the original input. If the single main-route producer failed or was skipped, the main experiment is NULL. Significant-variable boxplots with more than 25 retained rows require unique fitted variable names for ranking.

Available steps

Here’s the full lineup of available step functions:

Function Description Require Glycan Structure Experiment Type
Preprocessing
step_ident_overview() Summarize the experiment (identification overview) No GP/G
step_plot_qc() Generate quality control plots No GP/G
step_preprocess() Preprocess the experiment (normalization, imputation, etc.) No GP/G
step_zero_to_na() Convert zeros to missing measurements No GP/G
step_remove() Filter features by missingness, abundance, or variation No GP/G
step_normalize() Normalize sample abundances No GP/G
step_impute() Impute missing abundances No GP/G
step_aggregate() Combine measurements at a glycan, glycoform, or glycopeptide level Depends on level GP/G
step_detect_batch_effect() Save a table of batch effect p-values by feature No GP/G
step_correct_batch_effect() Correct batch effects automatically or with ComBat or limma No GP/G
step_transform_log() Store abundances on a logarithmic scale No GP/G
step_coda() Transform abundances to log-ratio coordinates for compositional data analysis No GP/G
step_subset_groups() Subset the experiment to specific groups No GP/G
step_adjust_protein() Adjust glycoform quantification by protein abundance No GP
Differential Analysis
step_dea_limma() Differential expression analysis using limma No GP/G
step_dea_ttest() Differential expression analysis using t-test No GP/G
step_dea_anova() Differential expression analysis using ANOVA No GP/G
step_dea_wilcox() Differential expression analysis using Wilcoxon test No GP/G
step_dea_kruskal() Differential expression analysis using Kruskal-Wallis test No GP/G
step_filter_sig_vars() Filter the fitted experiment by significance No GP/G
Visualization
step_volcano() Create volcano plot from DEA results No GP/G
step_heatmap() Create heatmap plot No GP/G
step_logo() Create logo plot for glycosylation sites No GP
step_plot_glycosite_profile() Plot distinct glycans per site and glycosylation sites per protein No GP
step_sig_boxplot() Boxplots for significant variables from DEA No GP/G

step_pca() Principal Component Analysis No GP/G
step_tsne() t-SNE analysis No GP/G
step_umap() UMAP analysis No GP/G
step_plsda() Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis No GP/G
step_oplsda() Orthogonal Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis No GP/G
Correlation & Enrichment
step_correlation() Pairwise correlation analysis No GP/G
step_sig_enrich_go() GO enrichment analysis on DE variables No GP
step_sig_enrich_kegg() KEGG enrichment analysis on DE variables No GP
step_sig_enrich_reactome() Reactome enrichment analysis on DE variables No GP
step_sig_enrich_ncg() NCG enrichment analysis on DE variables No GP

Choose individual preprocessing operations

Use step_preprocess() for glyclean’s full automatic workflow. To control the method or order, put the individual operations directly in the blueprint. For example, when zeros encode missing measurements, you can filter by missingness within each group, impute the retained features, and normalize each sample to its total abundance.

bp <- blueprint(
  step_zero_to_na() %=>%
  step_remove("rare", prop = 0.5, by = "group") %=>%
  step_impute("min_prob", seed = 42) %=>%
  step_normalize("total_area") %=>%
  step_plot_qc(when = "post", method = "rle", by = "group")
)

Each cleaning step reads the experiment on its incoming connection. The root input and intermediate experiments are available through cast_data(). Use method = "auto" for automatic selection within a single operation, such as imputation. For an explicit method, supply the arguments of the matching glyclean function. For example, step_impute("fw_knn", k = 3) calls glyclean::impute_fw_knn() with three neighbors.
